topics.name: Mexican-American War
topics.kicker: U.S. war with Mexico, 1846–1848 · Won California and the Southwest
topics.briefing: In 1846, the United States and Mexico went to war over Texas’s southern border, and President James K. Polk also wanted California. American armies under Zachary Taylor and Winfield Scott won battle after battle, and Scott captured Mexico City in 1847. In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Mexico gave up California and most of the present-day Southwest, but arguments over whether slavery would spread there helped lead to the Civil War.
topics.answerHtml: Mexican-American War (or Mexican War or U.S.-Mexican War; accept Intervención Estadounidense en México; do not accept “Spanish-American War”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This war began after Mexican cavalry attacked Captain Seth Thornton’s patrol of American soldiers in land claimed by both countries north of the Rio Grande. The American president then told Congress that the enemy had “shed American blood upon the American soil.”
tossups.r: That president was James K. Polk. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1846 to 1848 between the United States and its southern neighbor.

tossups.p: Before this war, the Mexican government refused to meet with John Slidell, whom the American president had sent to offer millions of dollars for California and New Mexico. That president then ordered General Zachary Taylor to march his army to the Rio Grande, into land that both nations claimed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that President James K. Polk led against Mexico from 1846 to 1848.

tossups.p: Early in this war, American cannons helped win the Battle of Palo Alto against Mariano Arista [“ah-REES-tuh”], and the Americans won again the next day at Resaca de la Palma [“reh-SAH-kuh day lah PAHL-muh”]. Nearby, an earthwork called Fort Texas was renamed for Major Jacob Brown, who died defending it.
tossups.r: Those victories were won by General Zachary Taylor. For 10 points, name this war that made Taylor a hero two years before he was elected president.

tossups.p: Jefferson Davis led the Mississippi Rifles at the Battle of Buena Vista [“BWAY-nuh VEE-stuh”] in this war, where an American army held off a much larger force led by Antonio López de Santa Anna. Months earlier, the same American general had captured the city of Monterrey [“mon-teh-RAY”].
tossups.r: That general was Zachary Taylor, nicknamed “Old Rough and Ready.” For 10 points, name this war fought from 1846 to 1848.

tossups.p: During this war, the U.S. Navy let an exiled general slip through its blockade and return home from Cuba, because the American president believed that general would help make peace. Instead, that general took command of his country’s army and fought against the United States.
tossups.r: That general was Antonio López de Santa Anna. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

tossups.p: In 1847, during this war, Winfield Scott landed thousands of soldiers on the beaches near Veracruz [“vair-uh-KROOZ”] in the first large-scale amphibious landing by U.S. forces. Scott then marched inland, roughly following the route that Hernán Cortés [“air-NAHN kor-TEZ”] had taken more than three centuries earlier.
tossups.r: Months later, Scott captured Mexico City. For 10 points, name this war fought under President James K. Polk.

tossups.p: At the Battle of Cerro Gordo [“SAIR-oh GOR-doh”] in this war, an army engineer named Robert E. Lee found a path through rough ground that let American troops get around the enemy’s side. Ulysses S. Grant, George McClellan, and Thomas “Stonewall” Jackson also served as junior officers in this war.
tossups.r: Many of those officers later fought against each other in the Civil War. For 10 points, name this earlier war that the United States fought from 1846 to 1848.

tossups.p: Mexico honors six young military cadets who died defending Chapultepec [“chah-POOL-teh-pek”] Castle in this war as the Niños Héroes [“NEEN-yohs AIR-oh-ays”], or “Boy Heroes.” U.S. Marines who stormed that castle are remembered in the line “From the Halls of Montezuma” in their hymn.
tossups.r: Right after that battle, American troops captured Mexico City. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

tossups.p: John Riley led the Saint Patrick’s Battalion, a unit of mostly Irish Catholic immigrants who left the U.S. Army and fought for the other side in this war. Many members of that battalion were captured at the Battle of Churubusco [“choo-roo-BOO-skoh”] near Mexico City.
tossups.r: They fought against the army of General Winfield Scott. For 10 points, name this war in which the United States won California and the Southwest.

tossups.p: The Army of the West under Stephen Kearny [“KAR-nee”] marched from Fort Leavenworth and captured Santa Fe without a fight early in this war. Kearny then headed for California, where the explorer John C. Frémont had joined American settlers rising up against Mexican rule.
tossups.r: This war added California and New Mexico to the United States. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1846 to 1848.

tossups.p: Pennsylvania congressman David Wilmot tried to ban slavery in any land the United States gained from this war. His proviso passed the House more than once but always failed in the Senate, and the fight over it split Northern and Southern lawmakers.
tossups.r: The argument over land won in this war led to the Compromise of 1850. For 10 points, name this war that ended in 1848.

tossups.p: Henry David Thoreau spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a tax, partly to protest slavery and this war. He explained his actions in the essay “Resistance to Civil Government,” later known as “Civil Disobedience,” which inspired Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which the United States gained a huge area from Mexico in 1848.

tossups.p: A one-term Illinois congressman introduced the “Spot Resolutions,” demanding that the president name the exact spot where American blood had been shed on American soil to start this war. Many Whigs attacked this conflict as “Mr. Polk’s War.”
tossups.r: That congressman, Abraham Lincoln, later became president. For 10 points, name this war in which General Winfield Scott captured Mexico City.

tossups.p: Nicholas Trist ignored orders calling him home and negotiated the treaty that ended this war. Under that treaty, the United States paid 15 million dollars for a vast area that included California, and the Rio Grande became the border of Texas.
tossups.r: That treaty was the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. For 10 points, name this war that ended in 1848.

tossups.p: Ulysses S. Grant, who fought in this war as a young officer, later called it “one of the most unjust ever waged by a stronger against a weaker nation.” The poet James Russell Lowell attacked this war in _The Biglow Papers_, written in the voice of a New England farmer.
tossups.r: This war began after the United States annexed Texas. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1846 to 1848.

clues.t: Fought from 1846 to 1848 between the United States and Mexico
President James K. Polk led the U.S. into it, hoping to gain California
Ended by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848): Mexico gave up California and most of the Southwest (the Mexican Cession)
Followed the U.S. annexation of Texas (1845) and a border dispute over the Rio Grande
Zachary Taylor (“Old Rough and Ready”) won at Palo Alto, Monterrey, and Buena Vista, then was elected president (1848)
Winfield Scott landed at Veracruz and captured Mexico City (1847)
Antonio López de Santa Anna led Mexico’s army
Wilmot Proviso (1846): tried to ban slavery in any land won from Mexico; passed the House but failed in the Senate
Congressman Abraham Lincoln’s “Spot Resolutions” challenged Polk to name where the war began
Polk told Congress that Mexico had “shed American blood upon the American soil”
Battle of Chapultepec (1847): Mexico honors its cadets as the Niños Héroes; the Marines’ Hymn recalls the “Halls of Montezuma”
Thornton Affair (April 1846): Mexican cavalry attacked Captain Seth Thornton’s patrol north of the Rio Grande
Mexico refused to meet John Slidell, whom Polk sent to buy California and New Mexico
First battles: Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma (1846) against Mariano Arista; Fort Texas was renamed Fort Brown
Jefferson Davis led the Mississippi Rifles at Buena Vista
Polk let the exiled Santa Anna slip through the blockade from Cuba, hoping he would make peace
Scott’s landing at Veracruz was the first large-scale U.S. amphibious landing; his march roughly followed Hernán Cortés’s route
At Cerro Gordo, engineer Robert E. Lee found a path around the Mexican flank; Grant, McClellan, and Stonewall Jackson also served
John Riley’s Saint Patrick’s Battalion, mostly Irish Catholic immigrants, fought for Mexico; many were captured at Churubusco
Stephen Kearny’s Army of the West took Santa Fe without a fight; John C. Frémont joined the uprising in California
Henry David Thoreau went to jail rather than pay a tax; he wrote “Resistance to Civil Government” (“Civil Disobedience”)
Nicholas Trist ignored his recall and negotiated the treaty: $15 million, with the Rio Grande as Texas’s border
Grant called it “one of the most unjust” wars; James Russell Lowell mocked it in _The Biglow Papers_
Many Whigs attacked it as “Mr. Polk’s War”

trap.title: Texas Revolution or this war?
trap.body: Texas shows up in two different wars. The Texas Revolution (1835–1836) is when Texas broke away from Mexico, with the Alamo, Sam Houston, and the Battle of San Jacinto. This war came a decade later, after the United States annexed Texas in 1845, and Santa Anna led Mexico’s army in both. Players also mix this war up with the Spanish-American War of 1898.
trap.fix: The Alamo, Sam Houston, or San Jacinto means the Texas Revolution. Polk, Zachary Taylor, Winfield Scott, the Wilmot Proviso, Chapultepec, or the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo means the Mexican-American War. Cuba, the Philippines, and “Remember the Maine!” mean 1898.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mexican-American War (or Mexican War; or U.S.-Mexican War)

topics.name: French and Indian War
topics.kicker: Britain vs. France for North America · Set the stage for the Revolution
topics.briefing: In 1754, a 22-year-old Virginia officer named George Washington led an attack that helped start a war over the Ohio River Valley. Britain and its American colonists fought France and its many Native American allies across North America until 1763. Britain won and took Canada, but its huge war debts led to new taxes on the colonies, which helped spark the American Revolution.
topics.answerHtml: French and Indian War (prompt on Seven Years’ War; accept Guerre de la Conquête)
reject: battle of the plains of abraham

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Seneca leader Tanacharison [“tan-uh-CHAR-ih-sun”], known as the Half King, guided Virginian soldiers to a French camp in a rocky glen in 1754, and the attack there helped start this war. The French officer Joseph Coulon de Villiers de Jumonville [“zhoo-mon-VEEL”] died in that attack.
tossups.r: Those Virginians were led by a young George Washington. For 10 points, name this war fought between Britain and France in North America from 1754 to 1763.

tossups.p: Weeks after an ambush that helped start this war, a young officer surrendered a small, hastily built fort to Louis Coulon de Villiers [“koo-LOHN duh vee-YAY”] on July 3, 1754. The surrender papers, written in French, said the officer’s men had committed an “assassination” in that earlier ambush.
tossups.r: That officer, George Washington, had surrendered Fort Necessity. For 10 points, name this war in which Britain took Canada from France.

tossups.p: In 1754, as this war was beginning, a Pennsylvania newspaper printed a cartoon of a snake cut into eight pieces, each labeled with the initials of a colony or region, above the words “Join, or Die.” Its creator proposed a plan at a meeting in Albany for the colonies to unite, but no colony approved it.
tossups.r: That creator was Benjamin Franklin. For 10 points, name this war in which Britain and its colonies fought France and its Native allies.

tossups.p: In 1755, General Edward Braddock’s army was ambushed and badly defeated near the Monongahela [“muh-non-guh-HEE-luh”] River while marching to capture Fort Duquesne [“doo-KAYN”] during this war. Braddock died days later, and the young wagon driver Daniel Boone escaped from that battle.
tossups.r: A young George Washington helped lead the retreat. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1763.

tossups.p: William Johnson, a British official who worked closely with the Mohawk, defeated and captured the French general Baron Dieskau [“DEES-kow”] at the Battle of Lake George in 1755 during this war. The Mohawk leader Hendrick Theyanoguin [“thay-uh-NOH-gwin”] was killed fighting on the British side in that campaign.
tossups.r: Johnson’s Mohawk allies belonged to the Iroquois Confederacy. For 10 points, name this war, the North American part of the Seven Years’ War.

tossups.p: During this war, British authorities forced thousands of French-speaking Acadians [“uh-KAY-dee-unz”] out of Nova Scotia, and many of them later settled in Louisiana, where their descendants are called Cajuns. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem _Evangeline_ tells of a young woman separated from her love during that expulsion.
tossups.r: This war ended with the Treaty of Paris of 1763. For 10 points, name this war in which Britain fought France for control of North America.

tossups.p: The Marquis de Montcalm [“mont-KAHM”] captured Fort William Henry in 1757 during this war, and his Native allies then attacked the British soldiers and families who were leaving under a promise of safe passage. James Fenimore Cooper’s novel _The Last of the Mohicans_ is set during that siege.
tossups.r: Montcalm later died defending Quebec. For 10 points, name this war in which Britain and France fought for North America.

tossups.p: In 1758, during this war, Montcalm’s much smaller French army defeated James Abercromby’s attack on Fort Carillon [“kah-ree-YOHN”], which stood between Lake George and Lake Champlain. The British captured that fort the next year and renamed it Fort Ticonderoga [“ty-kon-der-OH-guh”].
tossups.r: Ethan Allen captured that fort again in the American Revolution. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1763.

tossups.p: After British Secretary of State William Pitt poured money and troops into this war, John Forbes led an army across Pennsylvania in 1758. The French then blew up Fort Duquesne [“doo-KAYN”], which they had built at the Forks of the Ohio, rather than let Forbes capture it.
tossups.r: The British built Fort Pitt nearby, and the city of Pittsburgh grew around it. For 10 points, name this war fought over the Ohio River Valley.

tossups.p: Jeffery Amherst and James Wolfe captured the French fortress of Louisbourg [“LOO-iss-burg”] on Cape Breton Island in 1758, during this war. New England soldiers had already taken Louisbourg once in an earlier war, but Britain gave it back to France in a 1748 treaty.
tossups.r: The next year, Wolfe won the Battle of Quebec. For 10 points, name this war that ended French rule in Canada.

tossups.p: Benjamin West’s painting _The Death of General Wolfe_ shows a British commander dying on the battlefield during this war. In that 1759 battle, Wolfe’s soldiers climbed steep cliffs at night to reach the Plains of Abraham and defeated the Marquis de Montcalm, who also died.
tossups.r: That battle won Quebec City for Britain. For 10 points, name this war in which Britain conquered New France.

tossups.p: The Marquis de Vaudreuil [“voh-DROY”], the last governor of New France, surrendered Montreal to Jeffery Amherst in 1760, ending most of the fighting in North America during this war. That surrender came a year after the fall of Quebec City.
tossups.r: Three years later, France gave up Canada in the Treaty of Paris. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1754 to 1763.

tossups.p: In the treaty that ended this war, Britain chose to keep Canada and gave the sugar-rich island of Guadeloupe [“gwah-duh-LOOP”] back to France. Spain gave Florida to Britain in that 1763 treaty, after France had secretly handed Louisiana to Spain.
tossups.r: That treaty was signed in Paris. For 10 points, name this war that drove France out of mainland North America.

tossups.p: Soon after this war ended, the Ottawa leader Pontiac led an uprising against British forts near the Great Lakes, and the Proclamation of 1763 banned colonists from settling west of the Appalachian Mountains. To pay this war’s debts, Parliament passed the Sugar Act and the Stamp Act.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war between Britain and France that ended in 1763 and helped lead to the American Revolution.

tossups.p: Robert Rogers wrote a famous list of “Rules of Ranging” for his company of New England frontiersmen, who scouted and raided on snowshoes and in boats during this war. Rogers’ Rangers fought for the British around Lake George and Lake Champlain.
tossups.r: Their enemies were French soldiers and their Native allies. For 10 points, name this war fought in North America from 1754 to 1763.

Battle of the Plains of Abraham at Quebec (1759): James Wolfe beat the Marquis de Montcalm; both generals died

Afterward came Pontiac’s War, the Proclamation of 1763, and taxes like the Stamp Act to pay war debts
The Mohawk and, later in the war, most of the Iroquois Confederacy sided with Britain
James Fenimore Cooper’s _The Last of the Mohicans_ is set during the siege of Fort William Henry (1757)
The Seneca leader Tanacharison (the Half King) guided Washington’s men to Jumonville’s camp
Washington surrendered Fort Necessity to Louis Coulon de Villiers and signed a French paper admitting an “assassination”
Daniel Boone was a wagon driver in Braddock’s army
William Johnson defeated and captured Baron Dieskau at Lake George (1755); the Mohawk leader Hendrick was killed fighting for Britain
Britain expelled the French-speaking Acadians from Nova Scotia; many became Louisiana’s Cajuns (Longfellow’s _Evangeline_)
Montcalm beat James Abercromby at Fort Carillon (1758); the British later renamed it Fort Ticonderoga
John Forbes’s 1758 march made the French blow up Fort Duquesne at the Forks of the Ohio
Amherst and Wolfe took Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island (1758); New Englanders had captured it once before
Benjamin West’s painting _The Death of General Wolfe_; Wolfe’s men climbed cliffs at night to reach the battlefield
Governor Vaudreuil surrendered Montreal to Jeffery Amherst (1760), ending New France
In the 1763 treaty, Britain kept Canada over sugar-rich Guadeloupe; Spain gave Florida to Britain; France had secretly given Louisiana to Spain
Robert Rogers wrote “Rules of Ranging”; Rogers’ Rangers scouted on snowshoes

trap.title: Which colonial war?
trap.body: Britain and France fought four wars in North America, and this was the last and biggest. The first three were King William’s War, Queen Anne’s War, and King George’s War, and New Englanders even captured Louisbourg in King George’s War. Right after this war came Pontiac’s War (1763) and then the long road to the American Revolution, so clues about forts and Native alliances can point to several answers.
trap.fix: This war’s clues: Washington at Fort Necessity, Braddock’s defeat, the Albany Plan, Montcalm and Wolfe at Quebec, and the 1763 Treaty of Paris. Some answer lines accept the Seven Years’ War, the name for the whole worldwide war, but others only prompt on it, so say “French and Indian War” when the clues are in North America.
trap.line: Real answer line: French and Indian War (prompt on Seven Years’ War)

topics.name: Massachusetts
topics.kicker: The Bay State · Pilgrims, Puritans, and the first shots of the Revolution
topics.briefing: Massachusetts is where the Pilgrims landed in 1620, where Puritans founded Boston ten years later, and where the first shots of the American Revolution were fired at Lexington and Concord. It officially calls itself a commonwealth, and four presidents were born there, including John Adams and John F. Kennedy. Basketball and volleyball were both invented there, too.
topics.answerHtml: Massachusetts (accept Commonwealth of Massachusetts or Massachusetts Bay Colony; prompt on Massachusetts Bay Company)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: William Bradford served as governor of a colony in this future state for about thirty years and wrote a history of its founding. Before going ashore in 1620, 41 men of that colony signed an agreement to make “just and equal laws.”
tossups.r: Squanto helped those Pilgrims survive after they arrived on the _Mayflower_. For 10 points, name this New England state, home to Plymouth Rock.

tossups.p: In a 1630 sermon, John Winthrop told the Puritans sailing with him on the _Arbella_ [“ar-BELL-uh”] that their new colony would be “a city upon a hill,” watched by the eyes of all people. Winthrop’s colonists soon founded the town that became this state’s capital.
tossups.r: Winthrop served as that colony’s governor many times. For 10 points, name this New England state, whose capital is Boston.

tossups.p: Anne Hutchinson was put on trial and banished from this colony after she held meetings to discuss sermons and claimed to receive messages directly from God. In 1636, Roger Williams had fled this colony and founded Providence.
tossups.r: Both exiles settled in what became Rhode Island. For 10 points, name this “Bay State,” where Puritans founded a colony around Boston.

tossups.p: A 1647 law in this colony, nicknamed the “Old Deluder Satan Act,” required towns with at least 50 families to hire a teacher so children could learn to read the Bible. This colony’s legislature had also founded the oldest college in the United States in 1636.
tossups.r: That college, Harvard, is in Cambridge, across the Charles River from Boston. For 10 points, name this New England state.

tossups.p: Mary Rowlandson wrote a best-selling account of the months she spent as a captive after Native warriors raided her town of Lancaster in this colony in 1676. That raid came during a war led by Metacom, a Wampanoag [“wahm-puh-NOH-ag”] leader whom the English called King Philip.
tossups.r: Metacom was the son of Massasoit, who had helped the Pilgrims. For 10 points, name this New England state, where the Pilgrims had landed at Plymouth.

tossups.p: Tituba, an enslaved woman, was one of the first people accused during a 1692 panic in this colony, and Cotton Mather later wrote a book defending the trials that followed. Arthur Miller’s play _The Crucible_ retells those events, in which about 20 people were put to death.
tossups.r: Nathaniel Hawthorne, who was born in the town where those trials took place, set _The Scarlet Letter_ in this colony. For 10 points, name this state, home to the town of Salem.

tossups.p: In 1774, Parliament closed this colony’s main port until its people paid for destroyed tea, and it took away much of this colony’s power to govern itself. General Thomas Gage became this colony’s governor to enforce those Coercive Acts.
tossups.r: Colonists called those laws the Intolerable Acts. For 10 points, name this colony, where the Boston Tea Party took place.

tossups.p: Ralph Waldo Emerson’s “Concord Hymn” honors the farmers of this state who “fired the shot heard round the world” at a bridge in April 1775. On the night before that fight, Paul Revere and William Dawes rode out to warn that British troops were coming.
tossups.r: Those first battles of the Revolution were at Lexington and Concord. For 10 points, name this state, which honors them every April on Patriots’ Day.

tossups.p: Henry Knox hauled cannons from Fort Ticonderoga to Dorchester Heights, forcing British troops to leave this state’s capital on March 17, 1776. The year before, the British had won a costly victory nearby at Breed’s Hill, in a battle usually named for a different hill.
tossups.r: That battle was Bunker Hill. For 10 points, name this state, where the Revolution began at Lexington and Concord.

tossups.p: Elizabeth Freeman, known as Mum Bett, won her freedom in 1781 by suing under this state’s new constitution, which said that “all men are born free and equal.” After the Quock Walker cases, this state’s highest court ruled that slavery could not exist under that constitution.
tossups.r: John Adams wrote most of that constitution, the oldest written constitution still in use. For 10 points, name this New England state.

tossups.p: Governor James Bowdoin [“BOH-dun”] sent a militia under General Benjamin Lincoln to put down a revolt by farmers deep in debt in the western part of this state. In 1787, those farmers failed to capture the federal arsenal at Springfield.
tossups.r: That revolt, led by Daniel Shays, convinced many leaders to write a stronger constitution. For 10 points, name this state where four presidents, including both Adamses, were born.

tossups.p: A carved wooden fish called the “Sacred Cod” hangs in the chamber of this state’s House of Representatives. William King, who became Maine’s first governor, led the movement for Maine to separate from this state, which finally happened in 1820 under the Missouri Compromise.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England state, home to Cape Cod and the islands of Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard.

tossups.p: Young women who worked in this state’s textile mills wrote and published their own magazine, _The Lowell Offering_. Those mills, built by the Boston Associates, stood in a town named for Francis Cabot Lowell, who had memorized the designs of British power looms.
tossups.r: Those workers were called the Lowell mill girls. For 10 points, name this state, an early center of the Industrial Revolution in America.

tossups.p: William Lloyd Garrison began publishing his antislavery newspaper, _The Liberator_, in this state’s capital in 1831. During the Civil War, Robert Gould Shaw led this state’s 54th Regiment, one of the first official Black units in the Union Army, in an attack on Fort Wagner.
tossups.r: The 1989 film _Glory_ tells that regiment’s story. For 10 points, name this state, whose senator Charles Sumner fought slavery in Congress.

tossups.p: James Naismith invented basketball at a YMCA school in Springfield in this state in 1891, and William Morgan invented volleyball a few years later in nearby Holyoke. The first subway in the United States opened under the streets of this state’s capital in 1897.
tossups.r: That capital also hosts the Boston Marathon. For 10 points, name this state where John Adams and John F. Kennedy were born.

Harvard (1636), the oldest college in the United States, is in Cambridge

Maine was part of it until 1820, when Maine became a free state in the Missouri Compromise
Basketball (Springfield, 1891) and volleyball (Holyoke, 1895) were invented there; the first U.S. subway opened in Boston (1897)

William Bradford governed Plymouth for about thirty years; 41 men signed the Mayflower Compact (1620) before going ashore
It banished Roger Williams, who founded Providence (1636), and Anne Hutchinson; both settled in what became Rhode Island
The “Old Deluder Satan Act” (1647) made towns of 50 families hire a teacher
King Philip’s War (1675–1676), led by Metacom (son of Massasoit); Mary Rowlandson wrote about her captivity
Tituba was among the first accused at Salem; Cotton Mather wrote a book defending the trials
Emerson’s “Concord Hymn”: “the shot heard round the world”; Paul Revere and William Dawes rode to warn of the British
Henry Knox brought cannons from Fort Ticonderoga to Dorchester Heights, and the British left Boston (March 17, 1776); Bunker Hill was fought mostly on Breed’s Hill

Its 1780 constitution, written mostly by John Adams, is the oldest written constitution still in use

trap.title: Colony, city, or state?
trap.body: Massachusetts tossups use clues about places inside it that have their own answer lines: Boston (its capital), Plymouth Colony (the Pilgrims’ separate colony, which joined Massachusetts in 1691), Salem, and Cape Cod. Maine was also part of Massachusetts until 1820, so early Maine history can turn up in a Massachusetts question. Answering with the city or the colony when the question wants the state loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this city” is Boston, and “this colony founded by the Pilgrims” is Plymouth Colony. “This state” or “this commonwealth” is Massachusetts, and a question about John Winthrop’s Puritan colony takes Massachusetts Bay Colony or just Massachusetts.
trap.line: Real answer line: Massachusetts (accept Commonwealth of Massachusetts or Massachusetts Bay Colony)

topics.name: Reconstruction
topics.kicker: Rebuilding the Union after the Civil War · New rights for freed people
topics.briefing: After the Civil War, the United States faced two huge questions: how to bring the Southern states back into the Union, and what freedom would mean for about four million people who had been enslaved. During Reconstruction, three amendments ended slavery, made formerly enslaved people citizens, and protected Black men’s right to vote, and Black Americans were elected to Congress for the first time. Violence by groups like the Ku Klux Klan and the Compromise of 1877 brought it to an end.
topics.answerHtml: Reconstruction (accept Reconstruction Era; prompt on Reconstruction Acts or Reconstruction Amendments)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: During this period, Hiram Revels, a minister from Mississippi, became the first Black member of Congress when he took a seat in the U.S. Senate in 1870. Blanche K. Bruce, also from Mississippi, later became the first Black senator to serve a full six-year term.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this period from 1865 to 1877, when the former Confederate states were brought back into the Union.

tossups.p: Robert Smalls, who had escaped slavery by steering a Confederate ship to the Union navy, was elected to Congress during this period. P. B. S. Pinchback briefly served as governor of Louisiana in this era, becoming the first Black governor of a U.S. state.
tossups.r: Joseph Rainey became the first Black member of the House in 1870. For 10 points, name this period from 1865 to 1877.

tossups.p: General Oliver O. Howard led an agency during this period that set up schools, handed out food, and tried to make sure that formerly enslaved people got fair work contracts. A university in Washington, D.C., is named for Howard, who helped found it in 1867.
tossups.r: That agency, the Freedmen’s Bureau, was created in 1865. For 10 points, name this era when the federal government tried to rebuild the South after the Civil War.

tossups.p: In late 1865, Mississippi and South Carolina passed laws that forced freed people to sign yearly work contracts and let them be arrested for being unemployed. Those laws, which other Southern states copied, helped turn Northern voters against President Andrew Johnson’s lenient plan for this period.
tossups.r: Those laws were called the Black Codes. For 10 points, name this era after the Civil War, which ended in 1877.

tossups.p: William T. Sherman’s Special Field Order No. 15 set aside land along the coasts of South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida for freed families, in plots of up to 40 acres. That promise, remembered as “forty acres and a mule,” was mostly undone when President Andrew Johnson returned the land to its former owners.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this era after the Civil War, when the nation debated what freedom would mean for about four million people.

tossups.p: Senator Charles Sumner argued that the Confederate states had committed “state suicide” by leaving the Union, while Congressman Thaddeus Stevens said they should be treated as conquered provinces. Those two men led the Radical Republicans, who wanted a tougher plan for this period than the president did.
tossups.r: That president, Andrew Johnson, was impeached in 1868. For 10 points, name this period when the South rejoined the Union after the Civil War.

tossups.p: Abraham Lincoln pocket-vetoed the Wade-Davis Bill, which would have required a majority of a Southern state’s white men to take a loyalty oath before it could rejoin the Union. Lincoln’s own Ten Percent Plan for this process needed only ten percent of a state’s 1860 voters to swear loyalty.
tossups.r: Lincoln was assassinated before he could carry out his plan. For 10 points, name this process of rebuilding the Union after the Civil War.

tossups.p: Laws passed in 1867 over the president’s veto divided ten former Confederate states into five military districts, each run by a Union general. To be readmitted, each state had to write a new constitution that let Black men vote and ratify the Fourteenth Amendment.
tossups.r: Tennessee had already been readmitted in 1866. For 10 points, name this era, when Congress took control of rebuilding the South.

tossups.p: During this period, the House impeached President Andrew Johnson after he tried to fire Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, which Congress said violated the Tenure of Office Act. The Senate fell one vote short of removing Johnson, who had fought Congress over how to treat the defeated South.
tossups.r: Congress had earlier overridden Johnson’s veto of the Civil Rights Act of 1866. For 10 points, name this era from 1865 to 1877.

tossups.p: In the 1873 Slaughterhouse Cases, the Supreme Court gave a narrow reading to an amendment passed during this period, limiting the federal protection it offered. That amendment, ratified in 1868, declared that people born or naturalized in the United States are citizens and promised “equal protection of the laws.”
tossups.r: That was the Fourteenth Amendment, one of three amendments added in this era. For 10 points, name this era, which followed the Civil War.

tossups.p: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed an amendment of this period because it protected voting rights regardless of “race, color, or previous condition of servitude” but not sex. The fight over that 1870 amendment split the women’s suffrage movement into two rival groups.
tossups.r: That was the Fifteenth Amendment, the last of three amendments added in this period. For 10 points, name this era after the Civil War.

tossups.p: During this period, Congress passed the Enforcement Acts, including an 1871 law that let President Ulysses S. Grant use federal troops against a secret group that used violence and threats to keep Black people from voting. That group had been founded by Confederate veterans in Pulaski, Tennessee.
tossups.r: That group was the Ku Klux Klan. For 10 points, name this era when the federal government tried to protect freed people in the South.

tossups.p: During this era, the Supreme Court ruled in _Texas v. White_ that a state could not legally leave the Union. Opponents of this era’s new Southern governments mocked Northern newcomers as “carpetbaggers,” after the cheap bags some carried, and called white Southerners who worked with them “scalawags.”
tossups.r: Southern Democrats who took back their state governments called themselves “Redeemers.” For 10 points, name this era that ended in 1877.

tossups.p: After this period began, many freed families became sharecroppers, farming land owned by someone else in exchange for a share of the crop. Under the crop-lien system, store owners lent supplies against the next harvest, which trapped many of those farmers in debt.
tossups.r: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865, had abolished slavery. For 10 points, name this era that followed the Civil War.

tossups.p: A fifteen-member Electoral Commission gave 20 disputed electoral votes from Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon to Rutherford B. Hayes, who beat Samuel Tilden by one electoral vote. In the deal that followed, Democrats accepted Hayes as president, and he pulled federal troops out of Southern statehouses.
tossups.r: That deal after the 1876 election, the Compromise of 1877, ended this era. For 10 points, name this period after the Civil War.

clues.t: The era after the Civil War (1865–1877), when the former Confederate states were brought back into the Union
Three amendments: the 13th (ended slavery), 14th (citizenship and equal protection), and 15th (voting rights regardless of race)
The Freedmen’s Bureau (1865) set up schools, gave out food, and oversaw work contracts for formerly enslaved people
Ended with the Compromise of 1877, which made Rutherford B. Hayes president and pulled federal troops out of the South
President Andrew Johnson’s lenient plan clashed with Congress, which overrode his veto of the Civil Rights Act of 1866; he was impeached in 1868
Radical Republicans like Thaddeus Stevens and Charles Sumner wanted a tougher plan and stronger protection for freed people
Southern states passed Black Codes (1865–1866) to limit the freedom of formerly enslaved people
1867 laws split ten former Confederate states into five military districts and required them to let Black men vote
Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan; he pocket-vetoed the stricter Wade-Davis Bill (1864)
The Ku Klux Klan used violence and threats against Black Americans; the Enforcement Acts (1870–1871) let Grant send federal troops against it
Opponents insulted Northern newcomers as “carpetbaggers” and white Southern Republicans as “scalawags”
Many freed families became sharecroppers, often trapped in debt by the crop-lien system
“Forty acres and a mule”: Sherman’s Field Order No. 15 set aside coastal land, but Andrew Johnson gave it back to former owners
Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black member of Congress (Senate, 1870); Blanche K. Bruce was the first Black senator to serve a full term
Robert Smalls steered a Confederate ship to freedom and later served in Congress; P. B. S. Pinchback of Louisiana was the first Black governor of a state
Joseph Rainey of South Carolina: first Black member of the House (1870)
General Oliver O. Howard led the Freedmen’s Bureau; Howard University (1867) is named for him
Mississippi and South Carolina passed the first Black Codes (late 1865), with yearly work contracts and vagrancy laws
Sumner said the Confederate states had committed “state suicide”; Stevens called them “conquered provinces”
The Wade-Davis Bill would have required a majority of a state’s white men to take a loyalty oath
_Slaughterhouse Cases_ (1873): the Supreme Court read the 14th Amendment narrowly
Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed the 15th Amendment because it left out women; the suffrage movement split
The Klan was founded by Confederate veterans in Pulaski, Tennessee; an 1871 law let Grant use troops against it
_Texas v. White_ (1869): the Supreme Court ruled that a state could not legally leave the Union
Southern Democrats who took back their state governments called themselves “Redeemers”
1876 election: a 15-member Electoral Commission gave all 20 disputed votes to Hayes, who beat Samuel Tilden by one electoral vote
Tennessee was readmitted first (1866), so it was left out of the military districts

trap.title: Era or something inside it?
trap.body: Many answer lines live inside this era: the Freedmen’s Bureau, the Black Codes, the Fourteenth Amendment, Andrew Johnson’s impeachment, carpetbaggers, and the Compromise of 1877 all get their own tossups, and they share the same clues. If the question asks for “this era” or “this period,” say “Reconstruction,” but if it asks for “this agency,” “these laws,” or “this deal,” name that thing instead. The Reconstruction Finance Corporation, a 1932 Great Depression agency, is a different answer altogether.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun before you buzz. “This period” or “this era” after the Civil War means Reconstruction; “this agency” led by Oliver O. Howard means the Freedmen’s Bureau; “this deal” after the election of 1876 means the Compromise of 1877.

topics.name: Republican Party
topics.kicker: Major U.S. political party · Founded in 1854 to oppose slavery’s spread
topics.briefing: In 1854, people who wanted to stop slavery from spreading west met in a schoolhouse in Ripon, Wisconsin, and under a grove of oak trees in Jackson, Michigan, to start a new political party. Just six years later, its candidate, Abraham Lincoln, won the presidency. Nicknamed the “Grand Old Party,” or GOP, it is symbolized by an elephant that the cartoonist Thomas Nast made famous, and it has been one of America’s two major parties ever since.
topics.answerHtml: Republican Party (accept GOP or Grand Old Party; do not accept “Democratic-Republican Party”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Alvan Bovay suggested this party’s name at an 1854 meeting in a schoolhouse in Ripon, Wisconsin. That July, a convention of its supporters met outdoors “Under the Oaks” in Jackson, Michigan, because the crowd was too big for the hall.
tossups.r: Its founders wanted to stop slavery from spreading into the western territories. For 10 points, name this political party of Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: Thomas Nast’s 1874 cartoon “The Third-Term Panic,” printed in _Harper’s Weekly_, included a large animal labeled as this party’s vote. Nast kept drawing that animal to stand for this party, and it became the party’s best-known symbol.
tossups.r: That animal is the elephant, while the Democrats use a donkey. For 10 points, name this party of Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: This party’s first presidential candidate was an explorer nicknamed “the Pathfinder,” who lost the 1856 election to James Buchanan. That candidate, John C. Frémont [“FREE-mont”], still finished well ahead of former president Millard Fillmore, who ran for the Know-Nothings.
tossups.r: Four years later, this party won the presidency with Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this party founded in 1854.

tossups.p: Thaddeus Stevens and Charles Sumner led a “Radical” wing of this party that demanded strong protections for freed people after the Civil War. That wing pushed the Reconstruction Acts through Congress over President Andrew Johnson’s vetoes and led his impeachment in 1868.
tossups.r: This party’s first president had been Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this party whose symbol is the elephant.

tossups.p: In one election, this party’s nominee carried only Utah and Vermont after a former president from this party ran against him for the new “Bull Moose” Party. That split in 1912 let Woodrow Wilson win, even though William Howard Taft was the sitting president.
tossups.r: That former president was Theodore Roosevelt. For 10 points, name this party whose first president was Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: In 1872, a breakaway wing of this party nominated newspaper editor Horace Greeley against President Ulysses S. Grant, and the Democrats backed Greeley too. Twelve years later, reformers called Mugwumps left this party to support Democrat Grover Cleveland over its nominee, James G. Blaine.
tossups.r: Grant himself belonged to this party. For 10 points, name this party of Abraham Lincoln, whose symbol is the elephant.

tossups.p: Hiram Revels of Mississippi, the first African American to serve in the U.S. Senate, belonged to this party, as did Blanche K. Bruce, the first Black senator to serve a full term. During Reconstruction, most Black voters in the South supported this party.
tossups.r: Lawmakers from this party passed the 14th and 15th Amendments. For 10 points, name this party of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant.

tossups.p: Jeannette Rankin of Montana became the first woman elected to Congress when she won a House seat in 1916 as a member of this party. Decades later, this party’s Margaret Chase Smith of Maine became the first woman to serve in both the House and the Senate.
tossups.r: Its first president was Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this political party whose symbol is the elephant.

tossups.p: This party’s 1860 platform called for free western land for settlers, a railroad to the Pacific Ocean, and a protective tariff. During the Civil War, its lawmakers passed the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railway Act, both in 1862.
tossups.r: That platform also opposed spreading slavery into the territories, and its candidate, Abraham Lincoln, won. For 10 points, name this party.

tossups.p: Led by Newt Gingrich, this party campaigned on a “Contract with America” in 1994 and won control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years. In 1980, this party’s candidate, Ronald Reagan, defeated President Jimmy Carter.
tossups.r: Since the 2000 election, TV maps have usually shown the states this party wins in red. For 10 points, name this party of Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: From 1860 through 1928, this party won all but four presidential elections, losing twice each to Democrats Grover Cleveland and Woodrow Wilson. Its long run of victories ended when Franklin Roosevelt defeated this party’s president, Herbert Hoover, in 1932.
tossups.r: Dwight Eisenhower won the White House back for this party in 1952. For 10 points, name this party, whose first president was Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: Roscoe Conkling led this party’s Stalwart faction, which opposed civil service reform, yet a Stalwart president, Chester Arthur, signed the Pendleton Act in 1883. Later, Mark Hanna ran a “front porch” campaign for this party’s 1896 nominee, William McKinley.
tossups.r: McKinley beat William Jennings Bryan. For 10 points, name this party whose earlier presidents included Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: This party held its first presidential nominating convention in Philadelphia in 1856. It rose in the mid-1850s as the Whig Party collapsed, drawing in former Whigs, Free Soilers, and antislavery Democrats.
tossups.r: It was founded in 1854 to fight the Kansas–Nebraska Act. For 10 points, name this party of Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: In 1864, this party ran under the name “National Union” to welcome War Democrats, and it replaced Vice President Hannibal Hamlin with Andrew Johnson of Tennessee. That ticket easily defeated Democrat George McClellan in November.
tossups.r: Its president, Abraham Lincoln, was reelected. For 10 points, name this party whose symbol is the elephant.

tossups.p: Torch-carrying marching clubs called the Wide Awakes campaigned for this party’s candidate in 1860. Months earlier, that candidate had beaten the front-runner, William Seward, for this party’s nomination at a Chicago convention hall called the Wigwam.
tossups.r: That candidate, Abraham Lincoln, became this party’s first president. For 10 points, name this political party.

clues.t: Abraham Lincoln, elected in 1860, was its first president
Its symbol is the elephant; the rival Democrats’ symbol is the donkey
Founded in 1854 by people who opposed spreading slavery into the western territories
One of the two major U.S. political parties since the 1850s, along with the Democrats
Formed to fight the Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854), which let settlers in new territories vote on slavery (popular sovereignty)
First presidential candidate: the explorer John C. Frémont, “the Pathfinder,” who lost to James Buchanan in 1856
Rose as the Whig Party collapsed, drawing in former Whigs, Free Soilers, and antislavery Democrats
Its Radical wing (Thaddeus Stevens, Charles Sumner) led Reconstruction and the 1868 impeachment of Andrew Johnson
Split in 1912 when Theodore Roosevelt ran as the “Bull Moose” Progressive against William Howard Taft; Woodrow Wilson won
Ran as the “National Union” ticket in 1864, pairing Lincoln with Andrew Johnson, a War Democrat
Dwight Eisenhower (“I Like Ike”) won the White House back for it in 1952; Ronald Reagan won for it in 1980 and 1984
Since the 2000 election, TV maps have usually shown the states it wins in red
Alvan Bovay suggested its name at an 1854 meeting in Ripon, Wisconsin; a big convention met “Under the Oaks” in Jackson, Michigan
Thomas Nast’s 1874 _Harper’s Weekly_ cartoon “The Third-Term Panic” helped make the elephant its symbol
Won all but four presidential elections from 1860 through 1928, losing twice each to Grover Cleveland and Woodrow Wilson
Nominated Lincoln over the front-runner, William Seward, at the Wigwam in Chicago (1860)
The Wide Awakes, torch-carrying marching clubs, campaigned for Lincoln in 1860
1860 platform: free western land for settlers, a Pacific railroad, and a protective tariff; the Homestead and Pacific Railway Acts passed in 1862
In 1872, a breakaway wing nominated editor Horace Greeley against Ulysses S. Grant; the Democrats backed Greeley too
Mugwumps: reformers who left it in 1884 to back Democrat Grover Cleveland over James G. Blaine
Roscoe Conkling’s Stalwarts opposed civil service reform, but Stalwart president Chester Arthur signed the Pendleton Act (1883)
Hiram Revels, the first Black U.S. senator (1870), and Blanche K. Bruce, the first to serve a full term, were members
Jeannette Rankin of Montana, the first woman elected to Congress (1916), was a member; so was Margaret Chase Smith of Maine
William McKinley won in 1896 with a “front porch” campaign run by Mark Hanna, beating William Jennings Bryan
1994: Newt Gingrich’s “Contract with America” helped it win the House for the first time in 40 years
Held its first presidential nominating convention in Philadelphia in 1856

trap.title: Not Jefferson’s Republicans
trap.body: In the 1790s, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison founded the Democratic-Republican Party, which people at the time often called simply the “Republicans.” That party split apart in the 1820s, and Andrew Jackson’s wing became the Democratic Party. Abraham Lincoln’s Republican Party is a different party, founded in 1854, long after Jefferson died, so mixing the two up loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Clues from the 1790s to the 1820s (Jefferson, Madison, the election of 1800, the Federalists as rivals) mean the Democratic-Republicans. Clues from 1854 on (the Kansas–Nebraska Act, Frémont, Lincoln, Reconstruction, the elephant) mean the Republican Party. If a question asks for a faction, such as the Radical Republicans or the Stalwarts, name the faction instead of the whole party.
trap.line: Real answer line: Republican Party (accept GOP or Grand Old Party; do not accept “Democratic-Republican Party”)

topics.name: Vietnam War
topics.kicker: Cold War conflict in Southeast Asia · Ended with the fall of Saigon in 1975
topics.briefing: From the 1950s to 1975, Communist North Vietnam and its Viet Cong allies fought to unite the country under their rule, while South Vietnam and the United States tried to stop them. More than 58,000 Americans and, by most estimates, more than a million Vietnamese died, and protests against the war spread across American college campuses. The war ended in 1975, when North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon, the South’s capital.
topics.answerHtml: Vietnam War (accept Second Indochina War or American War; prompt on Indochina War; do not accept “First Indochina War” or “Korean War”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ngo Dinh Diem became the first president of the South after the Geneva Accords of 1954 divided his country at the 17th parallel. Diem was overthrown and killed in a 1963 coup as a Communist-backed guerrilla war against his government grew.
tossups.r: American leaders feared that losing this fight would make nearby countries fall like dominoes. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the fall of Saigon in 1975.

tossups.p: In August 1964, the destroyer USS _Maddox_ clashed with torpedo boats, and a second attack reported two days later probably never happened. Within a week, Congress passed a resolution letting President Lyndon Johnson use military force without a declaration of war.
tossups.r: That Gulf of Tonkin Resolution led to a huge buildup of U.S. troops. For 10 points, name this war against the Viet Cong.

tossups.p: Weeks after a surprise offensive that included an attack on the U.S. Embassy in Saigon, CBS anchor Walter Cronkite told TV viewers that the United States seemed “mired in stalemate” in this war. Soon afterward, President Lyndon Johnson announced he would not run for reelection.
tossups.r: That offensive began during the Lunar New Year holiday of Tet in 1968. For 10 points, name this war fought against the Viet Cong.

tossups.p: In May 1970, Ohio National Guard troops fired on a crowd at Kent State University, killing four students during protests against this war. Those protests had erupted after President Richard Nixon announced that U.S. troops were entering neighboring Cambodia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that sparked huge protests on American college campuses in the 1960s and 1970s.

tossups.p: Le Duc Tho [“lay duck TOH”] turned down the Nobel Peace Prize he was awarded along with Henry Kissinger for negotiating a cease-fire in this war. The two men worked out the Paris Peace Accords, which were signed in January 1973 and led to the withdrawal of U.S. combat troops.
tossups.r: Fighting went on without the Americans until 1975. For 10 points, name this war that ended when Saigon fell.

tossups.p: During Operation Frequent Wind, U.S. helicopters carried thousands of people out of a capital city as Communist troops closed in. Weeks earlier, Operation Babylift had flown thousands of orphans out of the same country.
tossups.r: That city, Saigon, fell to the North on April 30, 1975. For 10 points, name this war that ended with Saigon’s fall.

tossups.p: Daniel Ellsberg secretly copied a top-secret Defense Department history of this war and leaked it to reporters. In 1971, the Supreme Court ruled in _New York Times Co. v. United States_ that newspapers could go on printing that study, known as the Pentagon Papers.
tossups.r: The study showed that several presidents had not told the public the whole truth about this war. For 10 points, name this war fought against the Viet Cong.

tossups.p: Maya Lin was still a college student when she won the contest to design a memorial to this war’s American dead and missing: a black granite wall on the National Mall carved with more than 58,000 names. It was dedicated in 1982.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in Southeast Asia that ended with the fall of Saigon in 1975.

tossups.p: Trucks and porters carried supplies south along a network of jungle paths through Laos and Cambodia that was named for this war’s most famous Communist leader. American planes bombed that route for years but never managed to shut it down.
tossups.r: Those supplies helped the Viet Cong guerrillas in the South. For 10 points, name this war in which the North was led by Ho Chi Minh.

tossups.p: In March 1965, U.S. Marines waded ashore at Da Nang [“dah NANG”] as the first American ground combat troops sent to this war. That same month, Operation Rolling Thunder began more than three years of bombing raids on the Communist North.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that President Lyndon Johnson expanded after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution.

tossups.p: In a 1969 speech, President Richard Nixon asked the “silent majority” of Americans to back his plan for this war. That plan trained the South’s army to take over the fighting so that American troops could gradually come home.
tossups.r: Nixon had inherited this war from Lyndon Johnson. For 10 points, name this war fought against the Viet Cong.

tossups.p: Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over President Nixon’s veto in 1973, largely in reaction to this war. That law limits how long a president can keep troops in combat without approval from Congress.
tossups.r: Congress never formally declared this war against the Viet Cong and the North. For 10 points, name this war that ended in 1975.

tossups.p: Arguments that anyone old enough to be drafted for this war was old enough to vote helped pass the 26th Amendment, which lowered the voting age to 18. Boxer Muhammad Ali lost his heavyweight title after he refused to be drafted to fight in it.
tossups.r: A 1969 draft lottery used birthdays to decide who would be called first. For 10 points, name this war fought against the Viet Cong.

tossups.p: In 1968, U.S. soldiers on a “search and destroy” mission killed hundreds of unarmed villagers at My Lai [“mee LYE”], and Lieutenant William Calley was later convicted for his role. Back in 1965, the Battle of Ia Drang [“EE-ah DRANG”] had been the first major clash between U.S. troops and the North’s army.
tossups.r: General William Westmoreland commanded U.S. forces during those years. For 10 points, name this war against the Viet Cong.

tossups.p: Navy pilot John McCain spent more than five years as a prisoner of war, partly in Hanoi’s Hoa Lo [“hwah LOH”] Prison, which American captives nicknamed the “Hanoi Hilton.” He and hundreds of other prisoners came home in 1973, after a peace agreement was signed in Paris.
tossups.r: McCain had been shot down over the North in 1967. For 10 points, name this war that ended with the fall of Saigon.

clues.t: The Communist North (capital Hanoi) and the Viet Cong fought the South (capital Saigon) and the United States
Ended when Saigon fell to the North on April 30, 1975; the city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City
Tet Offensive (1968): surprise attacks across the South during the Lunar New Year turned many Americans against the war
Sparked huge antiwar protests in the U.S.; supporters of the war were called “hawks” and opponents “doves”
Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964): after clashes with U.S. destroyers, Congress let President Lyndon Johnson expand the fighting
Ho Chi Minh led the North until he died in 1969; the Ho Chi Minh Trail carried supplies through Laos and Cambodia
The Geneva Accords (1954) split the country at the 17th parallel after the French lost at Dien Bien Phu
Domino theory: U.S. leaders feared that if one country fell to communism, its neighbors would fall too
Paris Peace Accords (January 1973), negotiated by Henry Kissinger and Le Duc Tho, ended U.S. combat
Kent State (May 1970): Ohio National Guard troops killed four students during protests against the invasion of Cambodia
Richard Nixon’s plan trained the South’s army to take over the fighting as U.S. troops came home; he asked the “silent majority” for support (1969)
General William Westmoreland commanded U.S. forces (1964–1968) and sent troops on “search and destroy” missions
March 1965: Marines landed at Da Nang, and Operation Rolling Thunder began bombing the North (1965–1968)
Ngo Dinh Diem, the South’s first president, was overthrown and killed in a 1963 coup
The destroyer USS _Maddox_ clashed with torpedo boats in August 1964; a second reported attack probably never happened
After Tet, CBS anchor Walter Cronkite said the war seemed “mired in stalemate”; Lyndon Johnson then chose not to run again (1968)
Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers, a secret history of the war; _New York Times Co. v. United States_ (1971) let papers print them

Battle of Ia Drang (1965): the first major clash between U.S. troops and the North’s army
My Lai (1968): U.S. soldiers killed hundreds of unarmed villagers; Lieutenant William Calley was convicted
Maya Lin designed its memorial in Washington, D.C.: a black granite wall with more than 58,000 names (1982)
Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted (1967) and was stripped of his boxing title; the Supreme Court overturned his conviction (1971)

The 26th Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age to 18: anyone old enough to be drafted should be old enough to vote
