Le Duc Tho turned down the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize he was awarded along with Henry Kissinger
April 1975: Operation Babylift flew thousands of orphans out of the South, and Operation Frequent Wind used helicopters to evacuate Saigon

trap.title: Which Indochina war?
trap.body: Vietnam saw two big wars in a row. In the First Indochina War (1946–1954), Ho Chi Minh’s Viet Minh defeated France, winning the decisive Battle of Dien Bien Phu; this war came next, which is why it is also called the Second Indochina War. Players also mix it up with the Korean War (1950–1953), another Cold War fight between a Communist north and a U.S.-backed south.
trap.fix: French generals, Dien Bien Phu, and dates before 1955 mean the First Indochina War. The Gulf of Tonkin, Tet, the Viet Cong, Nixon’s “Vietnamization” plan, Kent State, and the fall of Saigon mean this war. The 38th parallel, Inchon, and Truman firing MacArthur mean Korea; the 17th parallel means this war.
trap.line: Real answer line: Vietnam War (accept Second Indochina War or American War; prompt on Indochina War)

topics.name: Benjamin Franklin
topics.kicker: Founding Father, printer, and scientist · Showed lightning is electricity
topics.briefing: Benjamin Franklin left school at 10, ran away from his printing apprenticeship at 17, and grew up to be one of the most famous people in the world. He flew a kite in a thunderstorm to show that lightning is electricity, invented bifocals and the lightning rod, and published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_. He also helped edit the Declaration of Independence, won France’s help in the Revolution, and signed the Constitution at 81.
topics.answerHtml: Benjamin Franklin (accept Ben Franklin; do not accept “Franklin Roosevelt” or “William Franklin”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man slipped letters under the door of his brother James’s print shop, pretending to be a middle-aged widow named Silence Dogood. After quarreling with James, he ran away from Boston to Philadelphia at age 17.
tossups.r: He later published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_. For 10 points, name this Founding Father who flew a kite in a thunderstorm.

tossups.p: This man’s club of tradesmen, the Junto, led him to start the Library Company of Philadelphia, a lending library paid for by its members. He also organized the Union Fire Company, a group of volunteer firefighters in that city.
tossups.r: He printed the _Pennsylvania Gazette_ and showed that lightning is electricity. For 10 points, name this Founding Father.

tossups.p: In 1774, Solicitor General Alexander Wedderburn publicly scolded this man before Britain’s Privy Council for leaking letters written by Massachusetts governor Thomas Hutchinson. Eight years earlier, this colonial agent had testified to the House of Commons against the Stamp Act.
tossups.r: He later helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris. For 10 points, name this Founding Father who published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_.

tossups.p: This printer’s woodcut “Join, or Die” showed a snake cut into eight pieces, each labeled with the initials of a colony or region. He published it in 1754, the same year he proposed a plan of colonial union at the Albany Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Pennsylvania Founding Father and inventor whose face is on the $100 bill.

tossups.p: Mozart wrote music for an instrument this man invented, the glass armonica, which is played by touching spinning glass bowls with wet fingers. This inventor never patented any of his creations, believing that people should share inventions freely.
tossups.r: His inventions included bifocals and the lightning rod. For 10 points, name this Founding Father.

tossups.p: As a colonial deputy postmaster, this man and his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain, printed a chart of the Gulf Stream to help mail ships cross the Atlantic faster. In 1775, he became the first Postmaster General under the Continental Congress.
tossups.r: He also published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_. For 10 points, name this Pennsylvania printer and Founding Father.

tossups.p: At the end of the Constitutional Convention, this delegate, the oldest there, said he now knew that the half-sun carved on George Washington’s chair was rising, not setting. Asked what kind of government the delegates had made, he reportedly answered, “A republic, if you can keep it.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 81-year-old Pennsylvania delegate who had earlier helped write the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: In a 1784 letter to his daughter Sarah, this man complained that the bald eagle was “a bird of bad moral character” and called the turkey a much more respectable bird. He wrote that letter while living in France as an American diplomat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Founding Father who published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_ and flew a kite in a storm.

tossups.p: In a 1789 letter, this man wrote that “in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.” In his last years, he served as president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society and signed its petition asking Congress to end slavery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Founding Father, a printer and inventor whose face appears on the $100 bill.

tossups.p: This scientist won the Royal Society’s Copley Medal in 1753 for the work described in his book _Experiments and Observations on Electricity_. He called a row of linked Leyden jars a “battery” and named the two kinds of electric charge “positive” and “negative.”
tossups.r: He also invented the lightning rod and flew a kite in a thunderstorm in 1752. For 10 points, name this American scientist and Founding Father.

tossups.p: This author’s unfinished autobiography describes his plan to master 13 virtues, such as temperance, silence, and humility. It also recalls how he first walked into Philadelphia carrying “three great puffy rolls,” while his future wife, Deborah Read, watched from a doorway.
tossups.r: He later published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_ and signed the Declaration of Independence. For 10 points, name this Founding Father.

tossups.p: Wearing a simple fur cap, this American diplomat became a celebrity in Paris while living in the nearby village of Passy [“pah-SEE”]. After the American victory at Saratoga, he signed the 1778 Treaty of Alliance that brought France into the Revolutionary War.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Founding Father who later helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris with John Adams and John Jay.

tossups.p: This man’s son William, the last royal governor of New Jersey, sided with Britain in the Revolution and was held prisoner by the Patriots. The two never truly made peace, but this man took William’s son, Temple, to France as his secretary.
tossups.r: Years earlier, William had helped his father fly a kite in a thunderstorm. For 10 points, name this Founding Father.

tossups.p: This man was the only Founder to sign the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Alliance with France, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution. He also served on the Committee of Five, which chose Thomas Jefferson to write the first draft of the Declaration.
tossups.r: He also invented bifocals and the lightning rod. For 10 points, name this Pennsylvania printer who published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_.

tossups.p: This man helped found an academy that grew into the University of Pennsylvania, and he worked with Dr. Thomas Bond to open the Pennsylvania Hospital. He also started the American Philosophical Society so that colonists could share scientific ideas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Philadelphia printer who wrote _Poor Richard’s Almanack_ under the name Richard Saunders.

clues.t: Flew a kite in a thunderstorm (1752) to show that lightning is a form of electricity
Published _Poor Richard’s Almanack_ under the pen name Richard Saunders (“Early to bed and early to rise…”)
Invented the lightning rod, bifocals, and a wood-burning stove
His face is on the $100 bill
Signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution
Ran away from his brother’s Boston print shop to Philadelphia at 17; printed the _Pennsylvania Gazette_
Published the snake cartoon “Join, or Die” (1754) and proposed the Albany Plan of Union
Minister to France during the Revolution: signed the 1778 Treaty of Alliance and became a celebrity in Paris
Negotiated the Treaty of Paris (1783), which ended the Revolution, with John Adams and John Jay
On the Committee of Five, which chose Thomas Jefferson to draft the Declaration of Independence
Oldest delegate (81) at the Constitutional Convention; said the half-sun on George Washington’s chair was a rising sun
Testified to Parliament against the Stamp Act (1766), which was repealed soon after
As a teenager, wrote the “Silence Dogood” letters, pretending to be a widow, for his brother James’s newspaper
Founded the Junto club, the Library Company of Philadelphia (1731), and the Union Fire Company (1736)
Helped found the University of Pennsylvania, the Pennsylvania Hospital (with Dr. Thomas Bond), and the American Philosophical Society
Invented the glass armonica, played on spinning glass bowls (Mozart wrote music for it); never patented his inventions
As a deputy postmaster, charted the Gulf Stream with his cousin Timothy Folger; became the first Postmaster General (1775)
Won the Copley Medal (1753); named a row of Leyden jars a “battery” and called the two charges “positive” and “negative”
Scolded by Alexander Wedderburn before the Privy Council (1774) for leaking Governor Thomas Hutchinson’s letters
1784 letter to his daughter: the bald eagle has “bad moral character,” and the turkey is more respectable
1789 letter: “nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes”
President of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society; signed its 1790 petition to Congress against slavery, though he had enslaved people earlier in life
His son William, the last royal governor of New Jersey, stayed loyal to Britain; the two never truly made peace
The only Founder to sign the Declaration, the Treaty of Alliance, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution
Reportedly answered “A republic, if you can keep it” when asked what kind of government the Convention had made
His _Autobiography_ lists 13 virtues and tells how he arrived in Philadelphia with “three great puffy rolls”

trap.title: Which Franklin?
trap.body: Several famous people have “Franklin” in their names. Franklin Delano Roosevelt was the 32nd president, Franklin Pierce was the 14th, and this man’s own son, William Franklin, was the Loyalist governor of New Jersey. Saying just “Franklin” works on this answer line, but naming the wrong Franklin, or answering with one of his pen names, loses the tossup.
trap.fix: The kite, _Poor Richard’s Almanack_, Philadelphia, the Albany Plan, France during the Revolution, and the $100 bill mean Benjamin Franklin. The New Deal and World War II mean FDR. A Loyalist governor who broke with his famous father means William Franklin. Don’t answer with a pen name like “Poor Richard” or “Silence Dogood”; give his real name.

topics.name: Harry S. Truman
topics.kicker: 33rd U.S. President · Led the nation from World War II into the Cold War
topics.briefing: Harry Truman was a Missouri farmer, a World War I artillery captain, and the co-owner of a men’s clothing store that failed in 1922. He had been vice president for only 82 days when Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945, making him president in the last months of World War II. He decided to use atomic bombs against Japan, led the country into the Cold War, and kept a sign on his desk that read “The buck stops here.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Kansas City political boss Tom Pendergast helped launch this man’s career, and he won a U.S. Senate seat from Missouri in 1934. During World War II, this senator led a committee that investigated waste in defense spending and was credited with saving billions of dollars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who became president when Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945.

tossups.p: This man’s running mate in 1948 was Kentucky senator Alben Barkley, who became known as “the Veep.” That year, this man crossed the country on a “whistle-stop” train tour, giving short speeches from the back of his train.
tossups.r: He later held up a newspaper wrongly saying Thomas Dewey had beaten him. For 10 points, name this president who won the 1948 election in an upset.

tossups.p: This president’s Executive Order 9981 ordered an end to segregation in the U.S. armed forces in 1948. That year, some Southern delegates walked out of his party’s convention, and the breakaway States’ Rights Democrats, or Dixiecrats, nominated Strom Thurmond.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat who won the 1948 election anyway, beating Thomas Dewey.

tossups.p: This president agreed with a reporter who called the fighting that began in June 1950 a “police action” under the United Nations. In 1951, he fired General Douglas MacArthur for publicly calling for a wider war against China.
tossups.r: MacArthur had led UN forces in the Korean War. For 10 points, name this president who succeeded Franklin Roosevelt.

tossups.p: Partway through one 1945 conference, British election results replaced Winston Churchill with Clement Attlee, who then sat across the table from this president. At that Potsdam Conference, this president casually told Joseph Stalin that the United States had a powerful new weapon.
tossups.r: Soon afterward, this president’s orders led to the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. For 10 points, name this 33rd president.

tossups.p: This man, whose middle initial does not stand for any name, commanded an artillery unit called Battery D in France during World War I. He then opened a men’s clothing store in Kansas City with his army friend Eddie Jacobson, but it failed in 1922.
tossups.r: He later became Franklin Roosevelt’s last vice president. For 10 points, name this Missouri politician who became the 33rd president.

tossups.p: This man’s 61st birthday was V-E Day, May 8, 1945, less than a month after he unexpectedly became president. He told reporters he felt “like the moon, the stars, and all the planets had fallen on me” when he took office.
tossups.r: He had been vice president for only 82 days. For 10 points, name this man who succeeded Franklin Roosevelt.

tossups.p: In _Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer_, the Supreme Court ruled that this president had no power to take over the nation’s steel mills to head off a strike. Justice Robert Jackson’s concurring opinion in that 1952 case became a famous guide to presidential power.
tossups.r: The seizure came during the Korean War. For 10 points, name this president who succeeded Franklin Roosevelt.

tossups.p: While the White House was being rebuilt, this president lived across the street at Blair House, where two Puerto Rican nationalists tried to kill him in 1950. White House police officer Leslie Coffelt died stopping the attack.
tossups.r: Two years earlier, this president had beaten Thomas Dewey in a surprise victory. For 10 points, name this president.

tossups.p: In 1948, this president’s old army friend and business partner Eddie Jacobson persuaded him to meet a Zionist leader who later became Israel’s first president. That May, this president recognized the new state of Israel just 11 minutes after it declared independence.
tossups.r: He also signed the Marshall Plan that year. For 10 points, name this president who took office after Franklin Roosevelt died.

tossups.p: During this president’s term, General Lucius Clay helped launch Operation Vittles, in which American planes flew food and coal into a city cut off by a Soviet blockade. That airlift lasted from 1948 to 1949, the same year the United States helped create NATO.
tossups.r: That city was West Berlin. For 10 points, name this president whose namesake doctrine promised to help nations resist communism.

tossups.p: Congress passed the Taft–Hartley Act over this president’s veto in 1947, limiting labor unions and banning the “closed shop,” where only union members could be hired. In his 1948 campaign, he attacked that Republican-led Congress as the “Do-Nothing Congress.”
tossups.r: His domestic program was called the Fair Deal. For 10 points, name this president who followed Franklin Roosevelt.

tossups.p: This president signed the National Security Act of 1947, which created the CIA and the National Security Council and made the Air Force a separate branch. That year, he chose George Marshall as his Secretary of State.
tossups.r: Also in 1947, his namesake doctrine promised aid to Greece and Turkey to contain communism. For 10 points, name this president.

tossups.p: In 1965, Lyndon Johnson signed the Medicare bill at this former president’s library in Independence, Missouri, and handed him the first Medicare card. Years earlier, this man had asked Congress for national health insurance as part of his Fair Deal.
tossups.r: He kept a sign on his desk reading “The buck stops here.” For 10 points, name this 33rd president.

tossups.p: This president was on stage in his home state when Winston Churchill gave his “Iron Curtain” speech at a small college in Fulton, Missouri, in 1946. Two years later, this president signed the European Recovery Program, which sent billions of dollars to rebuild Western Europe.
tossups.r: That program is better known as the Marshall Plan. For 10 points, name this president who succeeded FDR.

clues.t: 33rd President (1945–1953); took office when Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945
Ordered the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945), and Japan surrendered
Kept a sign on his desk that said “The buck stops here”
Beat Thomas Dewey in the 1948 upset, then held up a newspaper that wrongly said Dewey had won
His doctrine (1947) promised aid to Greece and Turkey to contain communism
Signed the Marshall Plan (1948): billions of dollars to rebuild Western Europe, named for Secretary of State George Marshall
Berlin Airlift (1948–1949): planes flew food and coal into West Berlin during a Soviet blockade
Sent U.S. troops into the Korean War (1950) and fired General Douglas MacArthur (1951)
Executive Order 9981 (1948) ordered an end to segregation in the armed forces; Southern “Dixiecrats” ran Strom Thurmond against him
Met Joseph Stalin and Winston Churchill (then Clement Attlee) at the Potsdam Conference (1945)
Called his domestic program the Fair Deal, which included a plan for national health insurance
The United States helped create NATO in 1949, while he was president
1948 “whistle-stop” train tour; his running mate, Alben Barkley, was nicknamed “the Veep”
Kansas City boss Tom Pendergast’s political machine helped launch his career; elected senator from Missouri (1934)
As a senator, led a committee that investigated waste in World War II defense spending
Ran a Kansas City men’s clothing store (a haberdashery) with Eddie Jacobson; it failed in 1922
Commanded Battery D, an artillery unit, in France during World War I
His middle initial, “S,” does not stand for any name
Vice president for only 82 days; said he felt “like the moon, the stars, and all the planets had fallen on me”
V-E Day (May 8, 1945), when Germany surrendered, was his 61st birthday
Recognized Israel 11 minutes after it declared independence (May 1948)
_Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer_ (1952): the Supreme Court said he could not seize the steel mills
Survived a 1950 attack by two Puerto Rican nationalists at Blair House; officer Leslie Coffelt died stopping it
Congress passed the Taft–Hartley Act (1947) over his veto; he campaigned against the “Do-Nothing Congress”
Signed the National Security Act (1947), which created the CIA and the National Security Council
Got the first Medicare card from Lyndon Johnson at his library in Independence, Missouri (1965)
Was on stage when Winston Churchill gave his 1946 “Iron Curtain” speech in Fulton, Missouri
Agreed with a reporter who called the Korean fighting a “police action” under the United Nations

trap.title: Truman, FDR, or Ike?
trap.body: Truman’s presidency comes between two other famous ones. Franklin Roosevelt led the country through most of World War II and went to Yalta, but he died in April 1945, so the Potsdam Conference, V-E Day, and the atomic bombs belong to Truman. The Korean War armistice was signed in 1953, after Dwight Eisenhower became president, but it was Truman who sent troops to Korea in 1950 and fired MacArthur.
trap.fix: Pearl Harbor, the New Deal, and Yalta mean FDR. Potsdam, the atomic bombs, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin Airlift, and firing MacArthur mean Truman. The Korean War armistice and the interstate highways mean Eisenhower. If a question asks for a policy (“this doctrine”), answer “Truman Doctrine,” not just his name.

topics.name: Henry Clay
topics.kicker: Kentucky senator and Speaker · Nicknamed “the Great Compromiser”
topics.briefing: Henry Clay of Kentucky was such a skilled deal-maker that he earned the nickname “the Great Compromiser.” He helped hold the Union together three times, with the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise Tariff of 1833, and the Compromise of 1850. He ran for president three times and lost every time, famously saying, “I would rather be right than be president.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1806 even though, at 29, he was younger than the Constitution allows. When he moved to the House of Representatives in 1811, he was elected Speaker on his very first day.
tossups.r: He later earned the nickname “the Great Compromiser.” For 10 points, name this Kentucky senator who proposed the Compromise of 1850.

tossups.p: Senator John Randolph of Roanoke insulted this man so harshly that the two fought a duel in 1826, though neither was hurt. Randolph was angry about the election of 1824, in which this man finished fourth but then helped John Quincy Adams win in the House.
tossups.r: Adams then made him Secretary of State, a deal Andrew Jackson called a “corrupt bargain.” For 10 points, name this Kentuckian known as the Great Compromiser.

tossups.p: In one election, this man’s supporters mocked his opponent by asking, “Who is James K. Polk?” His “Raleigh letter” opposing the immediate annexation of Texas cost him support, and he narrowly lost that 1844 race to Polk.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Whig leader and longtime Kentucky senator who proposed the Compromise of 1850.

tossups.p: Abraham Lincoln called this man “my beau ideal of a statesman” and delivered a eulogy for him in Springfield in 1852. That year, this man became the first person to lie in state in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol.
tossups.r: He had earned the nickname “the Great Compromiser.” For 10 points, name this Whig senator from Kentucky.

tossups.p: This senator’s “Omnibus Bill” fell apart in the summer of 1850 when opponents picked it to pieces. Stephen Douglas then split it into separate bills and got them passed after President Zachary Taylor died.
tossups.r: Those bills admitted California as a free state and passed a stricter Fugitive Slave Act. For 10 points, name this Great Compromiser from Kentucky.

tossups.p: In 1830, Andrew Jackson vetoed federal money for the Maysville Road, which would have run from the Ohio River to this man’s home city of Lexington, because it lay entirely within one state. The veto was a blow to this rival’s plans for federal roads and canals.
tossups.r: Those plans were part of his American System. For 10 points, name this Kentucky senator, the Great Compromiser.

tossups.p: This man joined John Quincy Adams and Albert Gallatin as an American negotiator of the Treaty of Ghent, which ended the War of 1812. Before that war, he and John C. Calhoun led the “War Hawks” who pushed Congress to fight Britain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Kentuckian who later helped pass the Missouri Compromise and the Compromise of 1850.

tossups.p: This man and John C. Calhoun worked out the Compromise Tariff of 1833, which slowly lowered tariff rates and ended the Nullification Crisis with South Carolina. Andrew Jackson had threatened force against that state, which had tried to cancel federal tariffs.
tossups.r: This man had also pushed high tariffs as part of his American System. For 10 points, name this Kentucky senator nicknamed “the Great Compromiser.”

tossups.p: This senator introduced the 1834 resolution in which the Senate censured Andrew Jackson for removing federal money from the Second Bank of the United States. Anger at “King Andrew” led this man and Daniel Webster to found the Whig Party.
tossups.r: He ran as the Whig nominee for president in 1844. For 10 points, name this Kentucky politician known as the Great Compromiser.

tossups.p: In 1832, this man urged the Second Bank of the United States to seek a new charter four years early so he could make the bank a campaign issue. Andrew Jackson vetoed the recharter bill and then defeated this man in that year’s presidential election.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Kentucky senator, later a leader of the Whig Party, known as the Great Compromiser.

tossups.p: This man presided over the first meeting of the American Colonization Society in 1816, a group that later helped found Liberia as a home for free Black Americans. He also enslaved dozens of people at his estate, Ashland.
tossups.r: He later served as that society’s president. For 10 points, name this Kentucky senator known as the Great Compromiser.

tossups.p: In 1821, this man worked out a deal over a clause in a new state’s constitution that tried to keep free Black people from moving there. A year earlier, as Speaker of the House, he had helped pass a compromise that admitted Maine as a free state.
tossups.r: That deal was the Missouri Compromise. For 10 points, name this Kentucky politician known as the Great Compromiser.

tossups.p: Told that a speech criticizing abolitionists might cost him the presidency, this man replied, “I would rather be right than be president.” He ran for president three times, in 1824, 1832, and 1844, and lost every time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Kentucky senator who helped work out the Missouri Compromise and the Compromise of 1850.

tossups.p: Born in an area of Hanover County, Virginia, called the Slashes, this man later campaigned as “the Mill Boy of the Slashes.” As a young lawyer he moved west to Lexington, where he built an estate called Ashland.
tossups.r: He later served as Speaker of the House and as Secretary of State. For 10 points, name this Kentucky senator nicknamed “the Great Compromiser.”

tossups.p: Nicknamed “Harry of the West,” this senator formed the “Great Triumvirate” with Daniel Webster and John C. Calhoun. In 1850, a dying Calhoun had another senator read aloud his last major speech, which opposed this man’s plan.
tossups.r: That plan became the Compromise of 1850. For 10 points, name this Kentuckian known as the Great Compromiser.

clues.t: Nicknamed “the Great Compromiser” for his deals between North and South
Senator from Kentucky; his estate, Ashland, was near Lexington
American System: a protective tariff, a national bank, and internal improvements like roads and canals
Proposed the Compromise of 1850, which admitted California as a free state
As Speaker of the House, helped pass the Missouri Compromise (1820); then, as a House member, worked out a second deal over Missouri’s constitution (1821)
In 1824 he backed John Quincy Adams in the House and became his Secretary of State; Jackson called it a “corrupt bargain”
Elected Speaker of the House on his very first day as a congressman (1811)
Led the “War Hawks” with John C. Calhoun before the War of 1812, then helped negotiate the Treaty of Ghent
Founded the Whig Party with Daniel Webster to oppose “King Andrew” Jackson
Said “I would rather be right than be president” (1839)
Formed the “Great Triumvirate” of senators with Daniel Webster and John C. Calhoun
Lost three presidential races: 1824, 1832 (to Andrew Jackson), and 1844 (to James K. Polk)
Appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1806 at age 29, younger than the Constitution allows
Fought a duel with Senator John Randolph of Roanoke in 1826; neither man was hurt
1844: Whigs mocked his opponent by asking “Who is James K. Polk?”; his Raleigh letter against annexing Texas cost him votes
His “Omnibus Bill” fell apart in 1850; Stephen Douglas passed its parts as separate bills
Ended the Nullification Crisis with John C. Calhoun through the Compromise Tariff of 1833
Led the Senate’s 1834 censure of Andrew Jackson for removing federal money from the national bank
Urged the Second Bank of the United States to seek an early recharter in 1832; Jackson vetoed it and beat him that fall
First person to lie in state in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda (1852)
Abraham Lincoln called him “my beau ideal of a statesman” and gave a eulogy for him in Springfield (1852)
Presided over the first meeting of the American Colonization Society (1816), which helped found Liberia; he also enslaved dozens of people
Born in the Slashes of Hanover County, Virginia (“the Mill Boy of the Slashes”); also nicknamed “Harry of the West”
Finished fourth in the 1824 Electoral College vote, so the House could not choose him
Andrew Jackson vetoed the Maysville Road (1830), which would have run to his home city of Lexington

trap.title: Clay, Webster, or Calhoun?
trap.body: Henry Clay, Daniel Webster, and John C. Calhoun were the “Great Triumvirate,” three senators who argued over tariffs, the bank, and slavery for decades, and all three appear in clues about the Nullification Crisis and the Compromise of 1850. Clay also shares clues with John Quincy Adams (the “corrupt bargain” of 1824) and with his great rival, Andrew Jackson.
trap.fix: Clay is the Kentucky deal-maker: the American System, the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise Tariff of 1833, and the Omnibus Bill. Webster is the Massachusetts speaker who said “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!”; Calhoun is the South Carolinian who defended nullification. Also skip Henry Clay Frick, the steel boss, and General Lucius Clay of the Berlin Airlift.
trap.line: Real answer line: Henry Clay (accept Henry Clay Sr.)

topics.name: James Monroe
topics.kicker: 5th U.S. President · Issued the Monroe Doctrine in 1823
topics.briefing: As an 18-year-old officer, James Monroe was badly wounded at the Battle of Trenton, and he went on to become the last Founding Father to serve as president. As the fifth president, he led the country during the “Era of Good Feelings,” acquired Florida from Spain, and warned Europe to stay out of the Americas with the Monroe Doctrine. He died on July 4, 1831, the third president to die on Independence Day.
topics.answerHtml: James Monroe (do not accept or prompt on “Monroe Doctrine”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While serving as minister to France, this man got Thomas Paine released from a Paris prison in 1794 and let Paine recover in his own home. George Washington later recalled this diplomat for failing to defend the Jay Treaty.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man whose 1823 namesake doctrine warned European powers not to start new colonies in the Americas.

tossups.p: In Emanuel Leutze’s painting _Washington Crossing the Delaware_, the soldier holding the flag is traditionally identified as this man. As a young officer, he was badly wounded at the Battle of Trenton, which followed that crossing.
tossups.r: He later became the fifth president. For 10 points, name this Virginian whose presidency was called the Era of Good Feelings.

tossups.p: This man argued against ratifying the Constitution at Virginia’s ratifying convention, and in 1789 he lost a race for the House of Representatives to James Madison. He later served as Madison’s Secretary of State before succeeding him as president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fifth president, who gave his name to an 1823 doctrine about the Western Hemisphere.

tossups.p: As governor of Virginia, this man called out the state militia in 1800 after learning of a planned revolt by enslaved people led by a blacksmith named Gabriel. He had earlier served as a U.S. senator and as minister to France.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who became the fifth U.S. president and issued a famous doctrine in 1823.

tossups.p: This diplomat and William Pinkney signed an 1806 treaty with Britain that Thomas Jefferson refused to send to the Senate because it did not end impressment. Three years earlier, Jefferson had sent this man to Paris to help Robert Livingston buy New Orleans.
tossups.r: Instead, they bought the whole Louisiana Territory. For 10 points, name this man who later became the fifth president.

tossups.p: After the British burned Washington in 1814, this man took over the War Department while still serving as Secretary of State, holding both jobs for the rest of the War of 1812. He had joined James Madison’s cabinet as Secretary of State in 1811.
tossups.r: He won the presidency in 1816. For 10 points, name this fifth president, whose 1823 doctrine warned Europe against new colonies in the Americas.

tossups.p: During this president’s 1817 goodwill tour of New England, the Boston newspaper _Columbian Centinel_ coined a famous phrase for the calm political mood of his time in office. During his presidency, the rival Federalist Party faded away.
tossups.r: That phrase was “the Era of Good Feelings.” For 10 points, name this fifth president of the United States.

tossups.p: In the 1820 election, William Plumer of New Hampshire was the only elector to vote against this president, choosing John Quincy Adams instead. The Federalists had not even nominated a candidate to run against him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president whose name is on an 1823 doctrine warning Europe not to colonize the Americas.

tossups.p: This president’s administration signed the Rush–Bagot Agreement, which limited warships on the Great Lakes, and the Treaty of 1818, which set much of the border with British Canada at the 49th parallel. His Secretary of State was John Quincy Adams.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fifth president, who presided over the Era of Good Feelings.

tossups.p: Luis de Onís [“oh-NEES”] negotiated an 1819 treaty with this president’s Secretary of State that drew a border with Spain’s lands all the way to the Pacific Ocean. Earlier, General Andrew Jackson had invaded Spanish Florida while chasing Seminole warriors.
tossups.r: In that treaty, Spain gave Florida to the United States. For 10 points, name this fifth president.

tossups.p: This president vetoed a bill to collect tolls on the Cumberland Road, arguing that the Constitution did not let Congress run such projects. The Panic of 1819, the country’s first major economic depression, struck during his first term.
tossups.r: He had won the presidency in 1816 as a Democratic-Republican. For 10 points, name this president of the Era of Good Feelings.

tossups.p: This president was nicknamed “the Last Cocked Hat” because he kept wearing the knee breeches and three-cornered hat of the Revolutionary era. He was the last of four early presidents from Virginia, a group called the Virginia Dynasty.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fifth president, who issued an 1823 doctrine warning Europe to stop colonizing the Americas.

tossups.p: This president died in New York City on July 4, 1831, exactly five years after John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died on the same holiday. He had studied law under Jefferson and later lived at Highland, a farm near Monticello.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fifth president, whose doctrine warned European powers to stay out of the Western Hemisphere.

tossups.p: The Supreme Court decided _McCulloch v. Maryland_ during this man’s presidency, and the Tallmadge Amendment set off a bitter fight over slavery in Missouri. That fight ended when he signed the Missouri Compromise in 1820.
tossups.r: Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, is named for him. For 10 points, name this fifth president.

tossups.p: Britain’s foreign secretary, George Canning, proposed that his country and the United States jointly warn other European powers away from Latin America. This president’s Secretary of State, John Quincy Adams, convinced him to make the statement alone instead.
tossups.r: That statement, in an 1823 message to Congress, became this president’s namesake doctrine. For 10 points, name this fifth president.

His namesake doctrine (1823) warned European powers not to start new colonies in the Western Hemisphere
His presidency was called the “Era of Good Feelings”
Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, is named for him
A Virginian, the last of the “Virginia Dynasty” of presidents (Washington, Jefferson, Madison, and him)
His Secretary of State, John Quincy Adams, wrote much of his famous doctrine and negotiated the Adams–Onís Treaty

Sent to Paris to buy New Orleans, he helped Robert Livingston buy the whole Louisiana Territory instead (1803)
Wounded at the Battle of Trenton (1776); traditionally said to be the flag-bearer in Leutze’s _Washington Crossing the Delaware_

As minister to France, got Thomas Paine released from a Paris prison (1794); Washington later recalled him over the Jay Treaty
Opposed ratifying the Constitution in Virginia, then lost a 1789 House race to James Madison
As governor of Virginia, called out the militia against Gabriel’s planned revolt of enslaved people (1800)
His 1806 treaty with Britain, signed with William Pinkney, was rejected by Jefferson because it did not end impressment

Vetoed a bill to collect tolls on the Cumberland Road (1822), saying Congress lacked that power

Nicknamed “the Last Cocked Hat” for still wearing knee breeches and a three-cornered hat
Studied law under Thomas Jefferson; his farm, Highland, was near Monticello

trap.title: The man, not the doctrine
trap.body: The Monroe Doctrine is its own common answer line, so it is easy to blurt out on a question about the man. On this answer line, “Monroe Doctrine” is wrong: the question wants the president himself. Players also mix him up with James Madison, the president just before him, since both were Virginians who served as Secretary of State before becoming president.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This president” or “this man” wants James Monroe; “this doctrine” or “this policy” wants the Monroe Doctrine. A John Quincy Adams tossup may mention the doctrine he wrote for his boss, and then the answer is Adams. Madison clues: “Father of the Constitution,” the Bill of Rights, and leading the country in the War of 1812; Monroe clues: the Era of Good Feelings, Florida, and the Missouri Compromise.
trap.line: Real answer line: James Monroe (do not accept or prompt on “Monroe Doctrine”)

topics.name: John Brown
topics.kicker: Radical abolitionist · Led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry
topics.briefing: John Brown was a white abolitionist who believed that only force could end slavery. In 1856, during the fighting known as “Bleeding Kansas,” he and his followers killed five proslavery settlers, and in 1859 he led a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to arm enslaved people. U.S. Marines led by Robert E. Lee captured him, and his raid and execution pushed the North and South closer to civil war.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: At a convention in Chatham, in what is now Ontario, this man presented a “Provisional Constitution” for a government he planned to set up after freeing enslaved people. A group of Northern backers called the Secret Six quietly paid for his plans.
tossups.r: In 1859, he led a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: Three days after proslavery forces raided the town of Lawrence in 1856, and two days after Senator Charles Sumner was attacked on the Senate floor, this man and his followers killed five proslavery settlers along Pottawatomie Creek.
tossups.r: That attack deepened the violence known as “Bleeding Kansas.” For 10 points, name this abolitionist who later raided Harpers Ferry.

tossups.p: John Steuart Curry’s mural _Tragic Prelude_ in the Kansas State Capitol shows this man with his arms stretched wide, holding a Bible in one hand and a rifle in the other, as a tornado and a prairie fire rage behind him.
tossups.r: This man led a raid on Harpers Ferry and was executed in 1859. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: This man’s raiders took Lewis Washington, a great-grandnephew of George Washington, as a hostage, along with a sword said to have belonged to the first president. The first person killed in the raid was Heyward Shepherd, a free Black railroad worker.
tossups.r: U.S. Marines led by Robert E. Lee captured him at Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: Henry David Thoreau gave a lecture in Concord defending this man, and Ralph Waldo Emerson also spoke in his praise. Both writers had met him when he visited Concord to raise money for his fight against slavery.
tossups.r: Weeks after Thoreau’s lecture, this man was executed for his raid on Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: Julia Ward Howe wrote new words to the tune of a Union marching song which said that this man’s body “lies a-mouldering in the grave.” Her new version of that song became the “Battle Hymn of the Republic.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this abolitionist who was executed after leading a raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859.

tossups.p: Frederick Douglass met this man at a stone quarry near Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, and refused to join his plan, warning that it would fail. This man also called Harriet Tubman “General Tubman,” though she did not take part in his attack.
tossups.r: That attack targeted the federal armory at Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: On the day of his execution, this man handed a guard a note predicting that “the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood.” He had been convicted of treason against the state of Virginia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this abolitionist who led a raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859.

tossups.p: In December 1858, this man led a raid into Missouri that freed 11 enslaved people, then guided them more than a thousand miles to freedom in Canada. Two years earlier, a battle at the Kansas town of Osawatomie had given him a nickname.
tossups.r: He later attacked the federal armory at Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: While running a wool business in Springfield, Massachusetts, this man organized Black residents into the League of Gileadites to resist the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850. His family’s farm was in North Elba, New York, where Gerrit Smith had given land to Black farmers.
tossups.r: He is buried on that farm. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who raided Harpers Ferry in 1859.

tossups.p: In his 1860 Cooper Union speech, Abraham Lincoln insisted that this man “was no Republican” and that no Republican had been tied to his attack. Many Southerners still blamed that attack on Republicans and other Northern opponents of slavery.
tossups.r: That attack was the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: In June 1856, this man’s fighters captured the proslavery militia leader Henry Clay Pate at the Battle of Black Jack. That August, his son Frederick was killed at Osawatomie, and two more of his sons later died in a raid he led.
tossups.r: That raid targeted the federal armory at Harpers Ferry in 1859. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: John Wilkes Booth joined a Virginia militia unit so he could watch this man’s execution in Charles Town. Cadets from the Virginia Military Institute also stood guard that day, led in part by a professor named Thomas Jackson, who later earned the nickname “Stonewall.”
tossups.r: That execution followed this man’s 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: Stephen Vincent Benét won a Pulitzer Prize for a book-length Civil War poem whose title comes from a marching song about this man. James McBride’s novel _The Good Lord Bird_ is narrated by a boy who travels with this man through Kansas.
tossups.r: In 1859, he led a famous raid on Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

tossups.p: Thomas Jefferson wrote that the view where the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers meet was “worth a voyage across the Atlantic.” In 1906, W. E. B. Du Bois’s Niagara Movement met at that spot and honored this man, whose raid had made the town famous.
tossups.r: That town is Harpers Ferry. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who led an 1859 raid on its armory.

A white abolitionist who believed violence was justified to end slavery
U.S. Marines led by Colonel Robert E. Lee captured him in the armory’s engine house

Fought proslavery settlers during “Bleeding Kansas” in the 1850s

A battle at Osawatomie, Kansas (1856), where his son Frederick was killed, gave him a nickname
In his Cooper Union speech (1860), Abraham Lincoln said he “was no Republican” and that no Republican had been tied to his raid

Freed 11 enslaved people in a Missouri raid (December 1858) and led them to Canada
Formed the League of Gileadites in Springfield, Massachusetts (1851), to resist the Fugitive Slave Act

His family’s farm was in North Elba, New York, near Lake Placid, where he is buried
The first person killed in the raid was Heyward Shepherd, a free Black railroad worker
His raiders took Lewis Washington, George Washington’s great-grandnephew, as a hostage
Captured the proslavery leader Henry Clay Pate at the Battle of Black Jack (June 1856)
Stephen Vincent Benét’s Pulitzer-winning poem takes its title from the song about him; he also appears in James McBride’s novel _The Good Lord Bird_
John Wilkes Booth joined a militia unit to watch his execution; VMI cadets, partly led by Thomas “Stonewall” Jackson, stood guard
W. E. B. Du Bois wrote a biography of him (1909); Du Bois’s Niagara Movement honored him at Harpers Ferry in 1906

trap.title: The man, not the town
trap.body: Many tossups ask for Harpers Ferry, the town he attacked, or for his raid, instead of the man himself. Clues like the federal armory, Robert E. Lee’s Marines, and the engine house show up in both kinds of questions, so a quick buzz with the wrong one loses the tossup. “Brown” alone only earns a prompt, because other Browns (like the _Brown v. Board of Education_ case) come up too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This man” or “this abolitionist” wants John Brown. “This town” or “this place,” where the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers meet, wants Harpers Ferry, and “this event” wants John Brown’s raid on Harpers Ferry. Say the full name, “John Brown.”
trap.line: Real answer lines: John Brown (prompt on Brown) and, for the town, Harpers Ferry

topics.name: Marbury v. Madison
topics.kicker: 1803 Supreme Court case · Established judicial review
topics.briefing: In his last days as president, John Adams rushed to appoint dozens of new officials, but some of their commissions were never delivered. When one of them, William Marbury, sued, Chief Justice John Marshall used the case to declare that the Supreme Court can strike down laws that break the Constitution. That power, called judicial review, helped make the Court one of the most important parts of the U.S. government.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This case struck down Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 because that law tried to give the Supreme Court more original jurisdiction than Article III of the Constitution allows. It was the first time the Court overturned an act of Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 Supreme Court case in which Chief Justice John Marshall established judicial review.

tossups.p: In this case, the Chief Justice declared, “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” He reasoned that when a law conflicts with the Constitution, judges must follow the Constitution.
tossups.r: That Chief Justice was John Marshall. For 10 points, name this 1803 Supreme Court case that established judicial review.

tossups.p: The plaintiff in this case asked the Supreme Court to issue a writ of mandamus, Latin for “we command,” ordering a cabinet officer to hand over a document. That document was a signed commission naming the plaintiff a justice of the peace in the District of Columbia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 case in which the Court claimed the power of judicial review.

tossups.p: After Congress repealed the Judiciary Act of 1801, it also canceled the Supreme Court’s 1802 term, so the justices did not hear this case until February 1803. Many Federalist judges lost their new jobs when that 1801 law was repealed.
tossups.r: The case grew out of John Adams’s last-minute “midnight judges.” For 10 points, name this case in which John Marshall’s Court established judicial review.

tossups.p: The Chief Justice who decided this case had, as John Adams’s Secretary of State, sealed the very commission at the center of the dispute but failed to get it delivered before Adams left office. That Chief Justice nevertheless ruled that the commission was valid.
tossups.r: That Chief Justice was John Marshall. For 10 points, name this 1803 case that established judicial review.

tossups.p: Former Attorney General Charles Lee argued this case for a plaintiff whom John Adams had named a justice of the peace. The defendant, the new Secretary of State, did not even send a lawyer to argue his side.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this case in which John Marshall declared that courts can strike down unconstitutional laws.

tossups.p: The opinion in this case asked three questions: whether the plaintiff had a right to his commission, whether the law gave him a remedy, and whether this Court could order the remedy he wanted. The answers were yes, yes, and no.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 case in which John Marshall established the power of judicial review.

tossups.p: After this case, the Supreme Court did not strike down another act of Congress until it ruled the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional in _Dred Scott v. Sandford_ in 1857. Both decisions found that Congress had gone beyond the powers the Constitution gave it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 case, John Marshall’s most famous decision, which established judicial review.

tossups.p: This decision argued that “a law repugnant to the constitution is void,” since the Constitution is the supreme law that every judge swears to uphold. It overturned part of a 1789 law that had organized the federal courts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this case in which Chief Justice John Marshall established judicial review.

tossups.p: This case ruled that Congress could not add to Article III’s short list of cases that go straight to the Supreme Court, such as those involving ambassadors or a state. So the Court could not give the plaintiff what he asked for.
tossups.r: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the opinion. For 10 points, name this 1803 case that established judicial review.

tossups.p: When Thomas Jefferson took office, his administration refused to deliver several commissions that John Adams had signed in his final days as president. One man who never received his commission sued the new Secretary of State in this case.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 case in which Chief Justice John Marshall established judicial review.

tossups.p: Alexander Hamilton had argued in _Federalist_ No. 78 that judges should treat the Constitution as a higher law than ordinary laws, an idea this case put into practice. This case’s opinion warned that a written constitution would mean nothing if Congress could ignore it.
tossups.r: John Marshall wrote that opinion. For 10 points, name this 1803 case that established judicial review.

tossups.p: Justice Samuel Chase, a member of the Supreme Court that decided this case, was impeached by the House the next year, though the Senate acquitted him. Thomas Jefferson’s allies distrusted the Court’s Federalist Chief Justice, whom John Adams had appointed.
tossups.r: That Chief Justice was John Marshall. For 10 points, name this 1803 case that established judicial review.

tossups.p: By ruling that his Court could not order the delivery of a commission, the Chief Justice avoided giving an order that President Jefferson would likely have ignored, while claiming a powerful new role for the courts. The plaintiff in this case never got his job.
tossups.r: That role was judicial review. For 10 points, name this 1803 case decided by John Marshall’s Court.

tossups.p: Seven years after this case, the same Chief Justice used _Fletcher v. Peck_ to strike down a Georgia law, one of the first times the Court overturned a state law. That Chief Justice, John Marshall, served longer than any other Chief Justice in American history.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 case, which established that federal courts can strike down acts of Congress.

trap.title: Which Marshall Court case?
trap.body: John Marshall’s Supreme Court decided several famous cases, and players mix them up. This case (1803) established judicial review; _McCulloch v. Maryland_ (1819) upheld the national bank and said “the power to tax involves the power to destroy”; and _Gibbons v. Ogden_ (1824) gave Congress power over steamboats crossing state lines. Some players also answer “judicial review,” which is the power this case established, not the case itself.
trap.fix: Midnight judges, an undelivered commission, a writ of mandamus, and Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 mean this case. A bank and a state tax mean _McCulloch_; steamboats and interstate commerce mean _Gibbons_. If the question says “this case,” name the case; “this power” or “this principle” wants judicial review.
